abstract: The BoRiabhach is a highly endangered traditional landrace cattle breed in Ireland with a culturally significant history. The Irish Gaelic word "riabhach" means "streaked", "striped", or "brindled", and a distinctive brindle coat colour pattern is characteristic of the BoRiabhach breed. The breed had declined to about 20 animals by 2016 and has no systematic pedigree. Despite conservation efforts that have increased the population to an estimated 70 animals, the breed remains one of Europe's most critically endangered livestock genetic resources. We present the first genomic characterisation of the BoRiabhach breed, using Illumina BovineSNP50 genotypes of 84 BoRiabhach animals and 688 cattle from 28 European comparator breeds. Using model-based clustering, we identified a BoRiabhach-specific ancestry component. Only 28 animals carried more than 50% of this component, which we term "high-BRBH"; the remaining 56 showed extensive introgression, chiefly from Limousin and Holstein, which explains the breed's high observed heterozygosity. Phylogenetic analysis placed the high-BRBH cohort with British Shorthorn and Lincoln Red within a British-Irish clade, distinct from Kerry and Dexter, and recovered a Limousin-to-BoRiabhach migration edge. This high-BRBH core group exhibited the lowest effective population size (Ne) of any adequately sampled breed and consists of closely related animals: 34% of pairs within the core were second-degree relatives or closer. Conservation of the BoRiabhach must therefore balance breed distinctiveness with genetic diversity. We recommend genotyping all extant animals, recording genomic ancestry at registration, managing mating based on genomic relatedness as well as ancestry, and cryopreserving germplasm from the high-BRBH core population.
